newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine big banks mixed on their prime rates.
newsitem.headline: Philippine big banks mixed on their prime rates.

text.p: The Philippines' five biggest domestic banks have adopted different positions on their prime lending rates despite a sustained decline in the country's benchmark interest rate, a Reuters survey on Tuesday showed.
The prime lending rate is the interest rate charged by banks to their top-tiered corporate clients.
The rate is adjusted according to the credit-worthiness of the borrower as well as the relationship between the bank and the client.
The Bank of the Philippines Islands (BPI) and Far East Bank and Trust Co said they had cut their prime rates.
But Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co (Metrobank), Philippine Commercial International Bank and Philippine National Bank (PNB) said they decided to keep their rates unchanged from last week.
The benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate has been falling for the past five weeks. It hit an 18-month low of 9.724 percent on Monday due to excess liquidity.
Analysts said they expected the rate to consolidate around the present levels in the near-term.
The Bureau of Treasury's deputy head, Eduardo Mendiola, said he projected the rate to remain soft in coming weeks following the low inflation scenario.

A BPI treasury official said the bank had cut its prime lending rate to 11.5 percent from 12.0 percent last week, while a Far East Bank official said its prime lending rate ranged from 11.5 to 12.5 percent "which is slightly lower than last week's".
But the country's biggest bank, Metrobank, decided to keep its prime rate unchanged at 12.0 percent.
"The rate has gone too low. We expect it to rebound especially if the U.S. Fed hikes its rate tonight," a treasury official at Metrobank said.
PCIBank said its prime rate was kept unchanged at 13.5 percent, while PNB said its rate was steady at 14.5 percent.
A PNB official said the rate had been at 14.5 percent since the early part of the year when the benchmark rate was hovering slightly above 11.0 percent.
Domestic banks review their prime lending rates every week after the treasury bills auction.
On Tuesday, the interbank call loan rate slipped to 10.03125 percent from 10.0625 percent after the Central Bank closed its overnight borrowing facility and withdrew its two-day reverse repos.
Bankers said they did not expect the Central Bank to make a move on its key rate until a decision on U.S. rates was out.
The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meets on Tuesday amid increasing speculation interest rates will be raised.
